President’s Message
by Don Gamble
Last month I wrote about the future of our workshop space
in the KMS Coquitlam building, and that KMS had given us
the green light for the Fall while they sorted out their new
warehouse. That has held, but we now have a firmer picture:
our time in the Coquitlam space ends on December 31.
The good news is that KMS has offered us space in their Ab
botsford store. Discussions are still under way, so nothing is
final yet, but the space looks very promising. It was formerly
a training room, it is considerably more modern than our
Coquitlam shop, and it has a rear entrance that will give
the Guild easy access. The board has approved a budget to
prepare the space, so we are ready to move forward as the
details come together.
KMS continues to be a generous partner. They have indicat
ed that they will transfer ownership of the tools, benches
and cabinets in the Coquitlam space to the Guild, and will
help us ship the large items on pallets. Owning the equip
ment, together with a formal lease for the new space, also
opens the door to grant funding that wasn’t available to us
before. There is still a lot of work to break down the existing
shop, and Brian Lunt has kindly agreed to lead it. Brian will
need help, so if you can lend a hand please speak to him
at the meeting or find his contact details in the member
directory.
Heather Marusiak’s visit is not affected by the move. Her full
day demo is on Saturday, October 24 at Sapperton Hall, and
you can join us in person or on Zoom. Please register on the
event page either way. Her workshops are at Lee Valley. As of
writing, there is still one seat open, so register soon if you’re
interested. If it’s gone, add your name to the waitlist, as we
may find a way to offer more seats. One note for the demo:
October 24 is also provincial election day, and the upstairs
of Sapperton Hall is being used as a polling station. Heath
er’s demo day goes ahead as usual on the lower floor, but
parking will be tight. Consider transit or a rideshare, or look
at your options ahead of time if you plan to drive.
Speaking of visiting demonstrators, Pippa Lattey, Art Liest
man and Cathy Nakagawa have done a great job and we
now have a full calendar of demonstrators lined up. There
is plenty of round and brown, along with some more artistic
turners, so they are keeping a good mix. I’ll share more
about the coming season later. For now, registration is open
for Dale Larson:
•
Saturday, February 20: Full day demo at Sapperton Hall
•
Sunday, February 21: Bowl Workshop
•
Monday, February 22: Sphere Workshop
•
Tuesday, February 23: topic to be confirmed

Editor’s Notes
by Britchie
Hello fellow woodturners.
We’ve a slightly lighter issue this month but still with some
entertaining anecdotes and edcuational contributions by
Lucas Siba and Mike Moult respectively.
We also have another healthy spread of member work in the
Instant and President’s Challenge galleries with some nota
bly creative examples by Dennis Houle (this month’s cover
feature), Malcom Cairns jointly with Paul Martin, and Theo
Vriezen to name a few.
You may also notice these galleries have been updated
with a new graphic layout designed to maintain the same
polished presentation of member work while reducing the
amount of time it takes to put these together. What would
assist in this effort would be if I could ask everyone who is
sending in work to do two things:
•
Make sure to include all info: for which gallery, title of
your piece, a brief description including any finishes,
sizing in inches (important).
•
Send-in your pics and info using the gallery@gvwg.ca
mailbox.
Thankyou all in advance.

E D I T O R S ’ S N O T E S
15% Discount for GVWG Members
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will only get
the store 5% non-Guild discount. By saying GVWG instead you
get the 15% Guild discount.
If you are buying something that needs a warranty, just give
them your Name and Address and that will go on the electron
ic file. If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is better
than the 15%, then you will automatically get the better rate.
Every purchase you make in the store by using this process
adds to our GVWG Credit account which we use to buy KMS
gift certificate prizes. We even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this! By doing this you are giving yourself
a better discount and helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out-of-town Guild member, all you have to do is
type in GVWG as the customer name when buying, and type in
your full name, address etc. in the ‘ship-to’ field and you will
get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the cost mar
gins from that manufacturer. This does not apply to published
special flyer items. If we all do this, we can even get up to a
bigger discount level in future!
[ K M S D I S C O U N T ]
DO tell them you are with the GVWG or Greater
Vancouver Woodturners Guild
DON’T give them your telephone number

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | O C T O B E R 2 0 2 6
Including
Inclusions
by Dennis Houle
It’s probably been over 10 years since I turned a hollow form; I
mainly turn bowls, with natural edge being my go-to favourite.
I’ve gathered suitable hollow form blanks over the years for
use “someday” which I’ve looked at periodically, but always
put them away for “another day”. This summer was the time to
get to work...
I turned a couple hollow forms out of clear Cherry and
Dogwood, with finials and pedestals, inspired by some of the
hollow forms I’ve seen by John Spitters.
When I looked at that Cherry blank with that large bark inclu
sion, I didn’t think it would suit a finial and I really wasn’t sure
how it would turn out. I mounted it between centers, turned it
round and trued-up the bottom. I screwed a waste block to a
4” faceplate and glued that to the bottom of the blank. I start
ed turning the top two-thirds using the golden mean principle
and made the largest diameter roughly one third from the top.
So far so good. The bark inclusion held together nicely and the
grain pattern looked great.
There were a few soft spots in the bark. I put a quick coat of
wipe-on-poly on the wood (not the bark) to protect the wood
from excess CA glue that would invariably run down and stain
the wood. Then I soaked the entire bark surface with thin CA
glue. There were a few long gaps along a joint between bark
and wood. I was concerned that a good portion of the bark
would blow out when I hollowed the inside. I really wanted
to keep the bark rather than have a gaping hole so I mixed
some System Three epoxy, thickened it with fine coffee grinds
and filled the gaps. It blended in nicely and held everything
together.
I left the bottom third about 4” diameter for now to keep the
blank solid while hollowing the inside. Then I drilled out the
blank with a 1 1/4” Forster bit down to about 3/8” from the
bottom. I hollowed out the inside to about a fat 1/4”. I could
have gone thinner as some more experienced turners will,
but I sure didn’t want to blow through the side (as I did on a
previous hollow form).
I finished turning the bottom third down to about same diam
eter as the opening (someone told me that was good design).
I sanded the outside to 600 grit. I also did some sanding on
the inside to get rid of ridges—more for the benefit of other
woodturners who will invariably stick their finger inside (we all
do it, don’t we?).
I finished with about 10 very thin coats of wipe-on-poly, that I
make up myself—regular polyurethane thinned down 50/50.
The first few coats just soak in. The finish doesn’t start to shine
until about the 4th coat. I put on very thin coats to avoid runs
using 2” gauze pads that I buy from Regency Medical in Burna
by….cheap and no fluff. I power sand with 1000 grit after every
2 or 3 coats, whenever it feels rough. I sand with 1500 grit after
the final coat.

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | O C T O B E R 2 0 2 6
85
M E M B E R A R T I C L E
The first sheet tore as I pulled it out of the package, before it
had touched a single shaving. I called it a fluke. The second
sheet survived the unboxing. It lasted about as long as a
sneeze before its grit wore off, and I was left sanding my bowl
with what was, technically, paper.
Inside the package sat a little drift of loose grit, like the sugary
dust at the bottom of a cereal box. I took it as a bonus, but it
was a confession. The glue holding the grit to the backing was
so weak that the paper was shedding before I’d used it. Bend
a good sheet back sharply and it hangs on to its grit. Bend a
cheap one and it snows.
Wrapped around the curve of a bowl, the stiff backing cracked
like an old road map, and on the spinning wood it fell apart.
Quality backings like tough paper or cloth flex and follow a
curve without complaint. My bargain paper hated curves,
which is a career-limiting attitude in a woodturning shop.
Then it clogged. Within minutes each sheet loaded up with
dust and turned slick, as if laminated. Clogged paper can’t cut.
The gaps between the grains were trapping dust, and once
they filled, you’re just rubbing. Better papers have coatings
that help them shed dust. Mine had nothing but optimism.
Even the clean patches dulled fast. Good grit is made to
fracture as it wears, exposing fresh sharp edges. Mine wore
down to tiny marbles and retired. My bargain power sanding
discs were no better. They ran hot, clogged, and roughed up
the very fibers they were supposed to smooth. Good abrasive
behaves the same way sheet after sheet. Mine had moods.
The scratch that would not die
The cherry bowl was supposed to be a gift. The tool work
came off clean, and I was proud of it. Then I spotted “the
scratch”. One deep, curving furrow that the next grit didn’t
touch. Neither did the grit after that. Three sheets later it was
still there, smirking at me.
Here’s what I learned. A grit number isn’t one size. It’s a range,
with most grains near the stated size and a few strays on either
side. Good manufacturers keep that range tight. Cheap paper
is a grab bag, and every so often the grab bag holds a boulder.
One oversized grain in a fine sheet plows a furrow the rest of
the sheet can’t fix. I named mine Gerald.
The defense starts at the store. Look for a “P” in front of the grit
number. It means the paper was graded to the European stan
dard, which allows less variation in grain size than the Amer
ican one. Good paper graded either way will serve you well;
the cheap stuff is where the boulders hide. But remember, at
the fine end of the two systems the numbers drift apart. So the
same number in two systems doesn’t always mean the same
size. Switching between them partway through can quietly
send you backward.
Thrift makes everything worse
Having paid so little, I was determined to get my money’s
worth. I kept using sheets long after they’d quit, armed with a
theory. A worn-out coarse sheet is basically a fine sheet. Free
grits!
Penny Wise,
Bowl Foolish
by Lucas Siba
It started as most of my bad decisions do,
in the clearance aisle. There it sat, a jumbo
variety pack of sandpaper, every grit from
“gravel” to “whisper,” priced like a typo. I
bought two. I drove home feeling like I’d
outsmarted the entire abrasives indus
try and told anyone within earshot that I
wouldn’t need sandpaper again until the
next ice age.
(Continues on the next page)

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | O C T O B E R 2 0 2 6
86
M E M B E R A R T I C L E
Wrong. Worn 120 is still 120. It’s just tired. Instead of cutting,
worn paper burnishes. The wood turns shiny, which looks
lovely and fools you completely, because the shine covers the
scratches and tool marks without removing them. I wasn’t
fixing my mistakes. I was polishing them.
Burnishing also makes heat, and dull, clogged paper makes
plenty. My fingertips got hot. The bowl got hot. At one point
the shop smelled faintly of toast. If the paper is getting hot, it’s
worn out (or you’re going too fast), and pressing harder only
makes it worse.
Heat does more than cook fingertips. It can scorch the wood
or open hairline cracks in the end grain called heat checks,
and cherry is one of the woods prone to them. You can’t sand
those cracks out. They run deeper than they look, and only a
sharp tool will remove them. So it was back to the gouge, then
back to the coarsest grit. My salad bowl became a cereal bowl.
Then the cereal bowl started becoming a ring dish.
Meanwhile, all that shed grit was busy. Loose coarse grains
stayed on the wood, got picked up by my finer sheets, and
dragged fresh scratches across surfaces I’d already finished.
That’s how you sand with a fine grit and get coarse-grit results.
The cure is wonderfully boring. Wipe the piece between grits
with a brush or give it a quick shot of compressed air.
The finish tells all
Eventually I had a bowl that looked smooth from across the
room, in dim light, if you squinted. I reached for the oil.
Finish is a truth serum. It won’t hide poor sanding, it will put it
on display. Every scratch I’d burnished over came roaring back.
A glossy finish works like a magnifying glass over every flaw.
Stain is worse still, it soaks into scratches and torn fibers and
outlines them like a crime-scene sketch. Sanding can’t save
poor tool work, but bad sanding will happily sink good tool
work.
I kept the bowl. It holds keys now. In fairness, it holds them
beautifully.
The bill comes due
Let’s tally the savings. I burned through the first jumbo pack
in record time. I spent hours re-sanding the same scratches,
re-turning heat checks. The bargain pack cost less per sheet
and far more per bowl.
Sandpaper is one of the smaller costs in this hobby. Skimping
on the one consumable that touches every surface of every
piece is false economy at its finest.
Lessons from the School of Hard Scratches
When I finally bought decent paper, the difference was almost
insulting. It cut. Dust poured off the bowl. Each grit erased the
scratches of the one before, just as the books promised. The
paper stayed cool, and so did I. Here’s what I’d tell my clear
ance-aisle self:
•
Sandpaper is a cutting tool – Keep it sharp, keep it clean,
and toss it when it’s dull.
•
Worn paper isn’t a finer grit – It burnishes, and burnishing
hides scratches instead of removing them.
•
Watch the dust – When it stops flowing off the piece, the
paper has stopped cutting.
•
Trust your fingertip – On the coarse and middle grits, fresh
paper drags. Compare your sheet with a new one.
•
Give it the bend test – if grit falls off at the crease, the
backing shows through, or loose grit sits in the package,
walk away.
•
Look for the P – Tighter grading means fewer boulders.
Be wary of mixing grading systems at the fine end.
•
Choose a backing that bends – Cloth or good paper fol
lows curves; cheap, stiff paper cracks.
•
Hot paper is a warning light – Slow the lathe and ease off
the pressure.
•
Wipe (or blow) between grits, and don’t skip any – Each
grit’s job is to replace the last grit’s scratches with smaller
ones.
•
Price is a hint, not a promise – Rock-bottom paper is
reliably bad, but the priciest sheet isn’t automatically the
best. Buy decent paper, run these tests, and believe what
your bowls tell you.
The rest of that second jumbo pack now lives in a drawer, a
monument to optimism and a reminder to keep learning.
(Continued from the previous page)

87
M E M B E R S P O T L I G H T
I saw my first lathe back in middle school many years ago. As
part of my woodshop course, I turned a block of wood into
what was supposed to be a bat. It simply looked like a slightly
round block of wood. Many years later, I took a pen turning
workshop at Lee Valley and I was hooked. It took me a few
more years before I had my own lathe and tools.
Currently, I consider myself a “fair weather turner”. I have a cor
ner of my yard walled off which we refer to as “Wood Hollow”.
On nice weekends, I haul my tools out and spend time there
making sawdust.
I like to work best with Cherry
or maple wood. I find fruit
woods or hard woods hold
an edge better. Realisti
cally, I will turn whatever
wood comes my way, which
includes branches from the
trees in my yard, wood peo
ple give to me, or donations
from the Guild meetings.
These days, I enjoy making
bowls or vessels. After I finish
a bowl, I usually apply a food
safe finish, such as Clapham’s
Salad Bowl Finish or How
ard’s Feed-n-Wax. This provides a lustrous finish for the bowl,
which can then be used as a presentation dish for food.
I like to augment the beauty of the wood with additional or
unique features. For instance, a few years ago, I took a maple
bowl and used pigment to color the outside azure blue and
the inside of the bowl gold. In another instance, I had a cherry
bowl and I wrapped the outside rim with copper wire in a tech
nique that I read about in a magazine.
Speaking of magazines, I forever have a wood turning mag

M E M B E R S P O T L I G H T
azine or book beside my bed. As I am a “fair weather” turner,
there are many long rainy nights, during the winter when I long
to be out in the sunshine, making shavings. Reading the mag
azines and books, helps take my mind off the day and leads
me to peaceful slumber.
At this point, I do not regularly sell my finished product. Earlier
on, when I was turning pens, I sold them at some local Christ
mas’s Crafts and at a local art gallery, but not currently. Now, I
give my bowls away to friends and family. Perhaps someday,
when I have more time, I can attend crafts shows or sell more
bowls. Many of my friends have encouraged me to set up an
online store to sell through. We’ll see how that goes.
Attending the GVWG
in-person meetings,
demonstrations and
courses is always a
treat. These events
provide opportunities
for me to learn from
people so I can ex
plore new techniques.
Experimenting like this
allows me to add to my
skill set and continue
my search to shape my
personal style. It is a
chance for me to con
nect with the wood and
the process of turning.
I turn because it feeds who I am. It is a deeply creative process
that allows me to explore a medium that has some perma
nence. At the end, I have created an item or artifact that will
hopefully go to someone, and when they see it, I hope they
will think of me for a moment.
Want to share your woodturning interests and practice?
Get in touch with Diana or email: editor@gvwg.ca

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | O C T O B E R 2 0 2 6
YOUR PERSONAL SAFETY
Always wear Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) such as
approved safety glasses or goggles that include side protec
tors. Use a full face shield for larger bowl, vessel, or any turning
involving chucks and faceplates. Wear a dust mask or an air
filtration helmet in conjunction with proper ventilation and/
or a dust collection system as appropriate. Remember—it’s
the fine airborne particles that are harmful to your respiratory
system. Wear hearing protection during extended periods of
turning.
Tie back long hair and avoid long sleeves or loose clothing.
Remove rings and other jewelry, or any dangling objects that
may catch on rotating parts or accessories.
Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close attention to
unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the
cause. Don’t operate machines when you are tired or under
the influence of drugs or alcohol.
WORKING SAFELY WITH YOUR LATHE
Ensure your workpiece is securely fastened. When using a
faceplate, be certain the workpiece is solidly mounted with
stout screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws as a minimum).
Do not use drywall or deck screws. When turning between
centers, check the workpiece is firmly mounted between the
headstock and tailstock and rotate your workpiece forwards/
backwards by hand to make sure it clears the toolrest and bed
before turning the lathe on.
Check all locking devices on the tailstock and tool rest as
sembly (rest and base) are tight before operating the lathe.
Check the speed of your lathe BEFORE turning it on. Use
slower speeds for larger diameters or rough pieces and higher
speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced.
Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is
balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the speed.
If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the machine to under
stand why. As a starting point, consult your operator’s manual
for recommended speeds for a particular lathe. Ensure the
lathe speed is compatible with the diameter of the blank.
Stay clear of danger zones directly behind and in front of the
workpiece. They are the most likely areas for a piece to travel
as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of
this zone when turning on the lathe, keeping your hand on the
switch in case you need to turn the machine off. When observ
ing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
Turn the lathe off before adjusting anything including the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches, and knock
out bars immediately after use. Never leave them in place,
even for a moment. Always remove the tool rest before sand
ing, finishing, or polishing operations.
Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced
woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and proce
dures not recommended for beginning turners.
Exercise extra caution when using stock with cracks, splits,
checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular shapes or protuberanc
es. Beginners should avoid these types of stock until they have
greater knowledge of working such wood.
Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding the tool
in a controlled but comfortable manner. Always contact the
tool rest with the tool before contacting the wood.
Never work with a lathe in reverse unless the chuck is using
a locking set-screw. It is possible for a chuck or faceplate to
unscrew unless it is fitted securely on the lathe spindle.
Don’t overreach. Keep proper footing and keep your balance

S A F E T Y G U I D E L I N E S
(Continues on the next page)
You mostly work on your own so safety is
YOUR responsibility. Please take the time to
read our safety guidelines and make them part
of your daily turning practice. Be safe out there!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | O C T O B E R 2 0 2 6
at all times.
Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer performance.
Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose for which
it was not designed or intended.
Consider your work environment. Don’t use a lathe in damp
or wet locations. Do not use in presence of flammable liquids
or gases, and always keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher
close at hand. Keep your work area well lit.
Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric cords for dam
age. Avoid the use of extension cords.
Never leave a lathe running unattended. Turn power off.
Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
SAFETY MAINTENANCE
Keep your lathe in good repair. Ensure belt guards or protec
tive covers are in place. Check for damaged parts, alignment,
binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect
its operation.
Read and follow safety guidelines for your lathe and other
workshop equipment. Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially bandsaws and chainsaws.

London Plane trees are large and stately. They have
been planted extensively in cities worldwide.
They have several distinctive features:
•
The tree sheds its bark in large patches giving the
trunks a characteristic mottled camouflaged ap
pearance.
•
The leaves are broad and flat (hence the name
plane tree) and resemble maple leaves.
•
The fruit consists of balls of seeds which hang on
long stalks.
•
London Plane trees trap and remove pollution and
shed it in their bark.
The trees help in urban cooling both in providing shade
and from evaporation. The pores in the leaves stay open
in hot weather
unlike most trees
which close. This
allows water to
evaporate giving
a cooling effect,
drawing water up
from the ground.
The London Plane
tree is a cross
between the
American Syca
more (Platanus occidentalis) and the Asian Plane tree
(Platanus orientalis). The American Sycamore is native
to the Eastern USA and the Asian Plane tree is native to
the Eastern Mediterranean and Iran. These were proba
bly crossed when they were introduced to Europe in the
1700s. The resultant hybrid is much more resilient to
drought, pollution and disease.
“Sycamores” found
locally will likely be Lon
don Plane trees. In Van
couver there are 2,327
London Plane trees, 4
American Sycamores
and 14 Asian Plane trees.
Confusingly the Ameri
can tree is called a Syc
amore while in Europe a
Sycamore refers to the
Sycamore Maple (Acer
platanus).
London Plane tree wood is similar to Maple. It is main
ly sapwood, straight grained and light in colour. The
heartwood is minimal and dark red. It is easy to ma
chine. Quarter sawn wood has marked figure from its
ray flecks giving it to be called lacewood. The wood is
moderately hard, Janka hardness 940.
